whyNext: Builds on LIFO stack mechanics from Valid Parentheses (Seq 69) by utilizing two stacks (inStack and outStack) to simulate FIFO queue operations with amortized O(1) push and pop.
hints: One stack handles incoming pushes, and the second stack handles outgoing pops and peeks.
When the outStack is empty, transfer all elements from inStack to outStack to reverse their order.
push(x): push to inStack. pop(): if outStack empty, transfer inStack to outStack; pop outStack. peek(): same transfer; peek outStack. empty(): both stacks empty.

brute.idea: Rebalance elements into a temporary stack on every single push operation to keep the queue head at the top.
steps: In push(x): transfer all elements from stack1 to stack2, push x onto stack1, transfer all elements back from stack2 to stack1.
In pop(): pop directly from stack1.
In peek(): peek directly from stack1.
In empty(): check stack1.isEmpty().
brute.whySlow: Moving all elements back and forth on every push takes O(n) per push.

optimal.idea: Two stacks: lazily transfer elements from inStack to outStack only when outStack is empty, achieving amortized O(1) operations.
steps: push(x): push x directly onto inStack.
pop(): call shiftStacks(); pop from outStack.
peek(): call shiftStacks(); peek from outStack.
shiftStacks(): if outStack is empty, while inStack is not empty, pop from inStack and push to outStack.
empty(): return inStack.isEmpty() && outStack.isEmpty().

whyNext: Inverts the adapter pattern from Implement Queue using Stacks (Seq 355) by using queue rotations to simulate LIFO stack operations with a single FIFO queue.
hints: To simulate a stack with a queue, the most recently pushed element must end up at the front of the queue.
When pushing a new element, enqueue it and then rotate the previous elements behind it.
push(x): add x to queue. For i from 0 to queue.size() - 2, poll an element and re-add it to the back. pop(): poll from queue. top(): peek from queue.

brute.idea: Use two queues: on pop, transfer n - 1 elements from q1 to q2, retrieve the remaining element, and swap references.
steps: push(x): add to q1.
pop(): while q1.size() > 1, transfer to q2; remove last element from q1; swap q1 and q2; return removed element.
top(): similar transfer, keep last element, re-add to q2, swap queues.
empty(): return q1.isEmpty().
brute.whySlow: Transferring elements on every pop or top takes O(n) time.

optimal.idea: Single queue rotation: upon enqueueing x, rotate the previous n - 1 elements behind x so x sits at the front.
steps: In push(x): add x to queue.
Loop size - 1 times: poll the front element and offer it back to the tail.
pop(): directly poll from front.
top(): directly peek front.
empty(): return queue.isEmpty().
optimal.time: O(n) push, O(1) pop and top

whyNext: Applies queue FIFO eviction from Implement Stack using Queues (Seq 356) by maintaining timestamps in a Queue and evicting calls older than t - 3000.
hints: Calls arrive with strictly increasing timestamps; a queue preserves this chronological order naturally.
Add the current timestamp t, then pop all timestamps from the front that are strictly less than t - 3000.
In ping(t): queue.offer(t). While queue.peek() < t - 3000: queue.poll(). Return queue.size().

brute.idea: Store all ping timestamps in a list and iterate through the entire list to count timestamps in [t - 3000, t].
steps: Append t to timestamps list.
Initialize count = 0.
Loop through all recorded timestamps: if ts >= t - 3000, count++.
Return count.
brute.whySlow: Scanning all past calls takes O(total calls) time per ping.

optimal.idea: Queue sliding window: enqueue t and discard elements older than t - 3000 from the front in amortized O(1) time.
steps: Add timestamp t to Queue.
While queue.peek() < t - 3000, dequeue the head element.
Return queue.size().

whyNext: Builds on stack top cancellation from Min Stack (Seq 68) by popping adjacent matching characters from a character stack to eliminate consecutive duplicate pairs.
hints: Process characters one by one using a stack.
If the current character equals the character at the top of the stack, pop it (they cancel out); otherwise push it.
Initialize StringBuilder as stack. For each c in s: if sb.length() > 0 and sb.charAt(sb.length() - 1) == c, delete last char; else append c. Return sb.toString().

brute.idea: Repeatedly scan the string to find and remove any adjacent duplicate pair until no duplicates remain.
steps: Initialize boolean changed = true.
While changed: set changed = false. Scan s for adjacent duplicate s[i] == s[i + 1].
If found: delete pair s[i..i+1], set changed = true, break to restart search.
Return resulting string.
brute.whySlow: Scanning and substring slicing repeatedly takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Single pass with a stack (or StringBuilder): push new char or cancel matching top in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize StringBuilder sb to act as a character stack.
For each character c in s: if sb has characters and sb.charAt(sb.length() - 1) == c, remove the top character.
Otherwise append c to sb.
Return sb.toString().

whyNext: Builds on stack cancellation from Remove All Adjacent Duplicates (Seq 358) by tallying unmatched closing brackets and remaining unclosed opening brackets.
hints: Track balance of open parentheses; unmatched closing brackets immediately demand an inserted open bracket.
Maintain openCount and addedCount. On '(', openCount++. On ')': if openCount > 0, openCount--; else addedCount++.
Total additions required is addedCount + openCount.

brute.idea: Simulate parentheses cancellation using an explicit stack of opening brackets.
steps: Initialize a Stack of Characters.
Initialize requiredInserts = 0.
For each char: if '(', push. If ')': if stack not empty, pop; else increment requiredInserts.
Return requiredInserts + stack.size().
brute.whySlow: Stack object allocation and boxing overhead for an O(1) counter problem.

optimal.idea: Count unmatched parentheses using two integer counters in O(n) time and O(1) space.
steps: Initialize open = 0 and needed = 0.
For each char in s: if c == '(', open++; else: if open > 0 open--; else needed++.
Return needed + open.

whyNext: Builds on unmatched bracket identification from Minimum Add to Make Valid (Seq 359) by recording invalid bracket indices and removing them to construct a valid parentheses string.
hints: Identify the indices of all invalid '(' and ')' parentheses.
Use a stack to track indices of unmatched '('; record unmatched ')' in a boolean or index set.
Pass 1: scan string, push index of '(' to stack; on ')', pop stack if non-empty, else mark index for removal. Add remaining stack indices to removal set. Pass 2: build string skipping marked indices.

Track indices of unmatched open parentheses in a stack.
For each ')', if stack is empty, mark char as empty; else pop stack.
Mark remaining indices in stack as empty.
Filter out empty chars and return string.

optimal.idea: Two-pass in-place marker: remove invalid ')' from left-to-right, then remove excess '(' from right-to-left in O(n) time.
steps: First pass: build intermediate StringBuilder sb1, tracking open count. Append characters; if ')' and open == 0, skip it; if ')' and open > 0, decrement open and append.
Second pass: scan sb1 backwards. If '(' and open > 0, decrement open and skip; else append to result.
Reverse result and return string.

whyNext: Builds on parentheses validation from Minimum Remove to Make Valid (Seq 360) by using an index stack initialized with base -1 to measure the maximum contiguous length of valid parentheses.
hints: A stack storing indices can measure the distance between the current valid end and the last invalid boundary.
Initialize stack with -1 to serve as a base marker for valid substrings starting at index 0.
For each index i: if '(', push i. If ')': pop. If stack empty, push i as new base; else maxLen = max(maxLen, i - stack.peek()). Return maxLen.

brute.idea: Check every even-length substring to see if it is a valid parentheses string.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to s.length() - 1.
Iterate j from i + 2 to s.length() with step 2.
Check validity of substring s[i..j-1] using a counter.
If valid, update maxLen = max(maxLen, j - i).
Return maxLen.
brute.whySlow: Checking all O(n²) even-length substrings takes O(n³) time.

optimal.idea: Stack storing indices initialized with -1 to measure valid spans in a single pass in O(n) time.

Initialize maxLen = 0.
For i from 0 to s.length() - 1: if s[i] == '(', push i.
If s[i] == ')': pop the top index. If stack is empty, push i (new boundary); else maxLen = max(maxLen, i - stack.peek()).
Return maxLen.

Evaluate the simple addition/subtraction expression inside.

class Solution:
    def calculate(self, s: str) -> int:
        stack = []
        res = num = 0
        sign = 1
        for c in s:
            if c.isdigit():
                num = num * 10 + int(c)
            elif c in "+-":
                res += sign * num
                num = 0
                sign = 1 if c == '+' else -1
            elif c == '(':
                stack.append(res)
                stack.append(sign)
                res = 0
                sign = 1
            elif c == ')':
                res += sign * num
                num = 0
                res *= stack.pop()
                res += stack.pop()
        res += sign * num
        return res

optimal.idea: Single-pass evaluation using an integer stack to save running sum and sign upon '(' in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize res = 0, num = 0, sign = 1, and Stack<Integer> stack.
Iterate through string: on digit, accumulate num = num * 10 + d.
On '+' or '-': res += sign * num; num = 0; sign = (c == '+') ? 1 : -1.
On '(': push res, push sign; res = 0; sign = 1.
On ')': res += sign * num; num = 0; res = stack.pop() * res + stack.pop().
Add trailing sign * num and return res.

whyNext: Builds on stack LIFO simulation from Min Stack (Seq 68) by greedily pushing elements from pushed and popping whenever the top matches the next expected popped element.
hints: Simulate the push and pop process using an explicit stack.
Iterate through pushed; for each element, push it onto the stack.
After each push, while stack is non-empty and stack.peek() == popped[j], pop from stack and increment j. Return stack.isEmpty().

brute.idea: Try all valid push/pop sequences to see if the target popped sequence can be produced.
steps: Model transitions: push next element or pop if possible.
Search state space (pushIdx, popIdx, stack).
If popIdx reaches popped.length, return true.
If all paths fail, return false.
brute.whySlow: State space search can branch exponentially without greedy matching.

optimal.idea: Greedy stack simulation: push elements and eagerly pop whenever top matches popped[j] in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>() and j = 0.
For each value x in pushed: push x.
While stack is not empty and j < popped.length and stack.peek() == popped[j]: pop and increment j.
Return j == popped.length.

whyNext: Builds on call-stack simulation from Validate Stack Sequences (Seq 363) by tracking function call intervals on a call stack and attributing elapsed time between timestamps to the active function.
hints: Use a stack to maintain the currently executing function IDs.
Track prevTime. When a new log arrives at timestamp, the function on top of the stack has been executing from prevTime to timestamp.

If log is 'start': add timestamp - prevTime to res[stack.peek()], push function ID, update prevTime = timestamp. If 'end': add timestamp - prevTime + 1 to res[stack.pop()], update prevTime = timestamp + 1.

brute.idea: Simulate each second of time by maintaining a call stack and recording which function was running at each second.
steps: Parse all events.
For each second t from 0 to maxTime, determine the active function at time t and increment its tally.
Return the array of execution times.
brute.whySlow: Simulating every second takes O(total duration) time.

optimal.idea: Stack tracking function calls, updating execution intervals on start and end events in O(logs) time.
steps: Initialize res array of size n, Stack<Integer> stack, and prevTime = 0.
Parse each log into id, type, and time.
If 'start': if stack is not empty, res[stack.peek()] += time - prevTime; push id; prevTime = time.
If 'end': res[stack.pop()] += time - prevTime + 1; prevTime = time + 1.
Return res.

whyNext: Builds on monotonic stack next-element searching from Daily Temperatures (Seq 72) by finding the next smaller or equal price to the right to compute discounted item prices.
hints: For each item i, find the first j > i such that prices[j] <= prices[i].
Use a monotonic increasing stack storing indices of prices.
Iterate through prices: while stack is non-empty and prices[stack.peek()] >= prices[i], idx = stack.pop(), res[idx] = prices[idx] - prices[i]. Push i.

brute.idea: For each item i, search linearly from i + 1 to n - 1 for the first price <= prices[i].
steps: Clone prices array into res.
For each i from 0 to n - 1, loop j from i + 1 to n - 1.
If prices[j] <= prices[i], res[i] = prices[i] - prices[j], and break.
Return res.
brute.whySlow: Searching forward for each element takes O(n²) worst-case time.

optimal.idea: Monotonic stack storing indices: resolve discounts when encountering a smaller or equal price in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize res = prices.clone() and Stack<Integer> stack.
For i from 0 to prices.length - 1: while stack not empty and prices[stack.peek()] >= prices[i], idx = stack.pop(), res[idx] -= prices[i].
Push i onto stack.
Return res.

Scan from right to left, keeping track of candidate values for nums[k] using a monotonic stack.
Maintain third = -infinity. Scan i from n - 1 down to 0: if nums[i] < third, return true. While stack not empty and nums[i] > stack.peek(), third = stack.pop(). Push nums[i]. Return false.

Iterate j from i + 1 to n - 2.

Scan i from nums.length - 1 down to 0.
If nums[i] < third, a '132' pattern is found; return true.
While stack is not empty and nums[i] > stack.peek(): third = stack.pop().
Push nums[i] onto stack.
Return false if loop terminates.

whyNext: Builds on histogram boundary expansion from Largest Rectangle in Histogram (Seq 76) by using monotonic stacks to find previous and next smaller element spans for each item, accumulating arr[i] * leftCount * rightCount.
hints: Each element arr[i] is the minimum in (i - prevSmaller) * (nextSmaller - i) distinct subarrays.
Find previous strictly smaller element and next smaller or equal element using monotonic stacks.
For each i: left = i - prevSmaller[i], right = nextSmaller[i] - i. Contribution is (left * right % MOD) * arr[i] % MOD. Sum contributions modulo 10^9 + 7.

brute.idea: Iterate all subarrays, compute the minimum of each subarray, and sum them modulo 10^9 + 7.
steps: Initialize total = 0, MOD = 10^9 + 7.
For i from 0 to n - 1: set min = arr[i].
For j from i to n - 1: min = min(min, arr[j]), total = (total + min) % MOD.
Return total.
brute.whySlow: Iterating through all O(n²) subarrays takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Monotonic stack calculating left and right dominance spans for each element in O(n) time.
steps: Calculate prevSmaller[i]: count of elements to left where arr[j] >= arr[i].
Calculate nextSmaller[i]: count of elements to right where arr[j] > arr[i].
Multiply arr[i] * leftCount * rightCount for each element.
Sum all products modulo 10^9 + 7 and return.

whyNext: Builds on monotonic queue extrema maintenance from Sliding Window Maximum (Seq 48) by utilizing two monotonic deques (maxDeque and minDeque) to maintain max - min <= limit over a flexible sliding window.
hints: Maintain both the maximum and minimum of the sliding window in O(1) amortized time using two deques.
Expand right edge. While maxDeque.peekFirst() - minDeque.peekFirst() > limit, shrink left edge.
Update maxLen = max(maxLen, right - left + 1).

brute.idea: Test every subarray [i, j], compute its max and min values, and check if max - min <= limit.
steps: Iterate i from 0 to n - 1.
Maintain min = nums[i] and max = nums[i].
For j from i to n - 1: min = min(min, nums[j]), max = max(max, nums[j]).
If max - min <= limit, maxLen = max(maxLen, j - i + 1); else break.
Return maxLen.
brute.whySlow: Testing all subarrays takes O(n²) time.

optimal.idea: Sliding window with two monotonic deques tracking window maximum and minimum in O(n) time.
steps: Initialize Deque<Integer> maxQ and minQ, and pointer left = 0.
For right from 0 to nums.length - 1: maintain monotonic decreasing maxQ and monotonic increasing minQ.
While maxQ.peekFirst() - minQ.peekFirst() > limit: if maxQ.peekFirst() == nums[left] maxQ.pollFirst(); if minQ.peekFirst() == nums[left] minQ.pollFirst(); left++.
Track maxLen = max(maxLen, right - left + 1).
Return maxLen.
